ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
NABARD Assistance for Cold Storage Units in Karnataka 
*501. SHRI K.C. KONDAIAH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Karnataka Government has sought financial assistance from 
National Bank for Agricultural and Rural Development to establish cold 
storage Units in rural areas of the State; 
(b) if so, the amount of financial assistance sought for; 
(c) the action, if any, taken in this regard; and 
(d) how many cold storage units are proposed to be set-up in rural areas of the 
State to preserve agricultural and horticultural produce? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The Karnataka Government has not sought any financial assistance 
from National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) for 
construction of cold storage in the rural areas of the State under the "Capital 
Investment Subsidy Scheme for Construction/Expansion/Modernisation of Cold 
Storages and Storages for Horticulture Produce" being implemented by the 
National Horticulture Board (NHB). However, NABARD has received 9 
projects for approval from Banks under the said NHB Scheme of private 
entrepreneurs for establishment of cold storages in Karnataka, out of which 7 
projects have been sanctioned involving a capacity  creation  of 25900  metric  
tonnes.   All  these  sanctioned 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [20 April, 2001] 
projects are proposed to be set up in rural areas. The component of bank loan 
of the sanctioned projects is Rs. 6.21  crores and NABARD will provide a 
refinance @ 90% of the bank loan i.e. Rs. 5.59 crores to the banks. The 
subsidy component eligible under the above mentioned capital subsidy 
scheme would be Rs. 2.84 crores. In respect of remaining two proposals 
NABARD after scrutiny have asked for additional information from the 
concerned banks. In addition NHB has sanctioned one project for being set 
up in Karnataka of 1000 metric tonne capacity for which a subsidy of Rs. 10 
lakhs has already been provided by the NHB.

ber (%), anjur, Chikoo, etc. These varieties have been developed by farmers 
on their own capacity and in their own interest, they are growing them on 
their own. But, unfortunately, the Department is not providing them any

thinking of setting up Horticultural Parks on the lines of Information 
Technology Parks, at least one in each di strict so that they are provided with 
all the infrastructure for storing the fruits and flowers for export purposes.

*504. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the current status of the Crocodile breeding programmes in Orissa, 
with details thereof; and 
(b) what specific steps Government of India have taken to revive the 
closed programmes? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU) (a) and (b) 
Crocodile breeding programme is being carried out in Orissa at Tikarpada, 
Dangmal and Ramatirtha for ghaxial, estuarine crocodile and the magar 
respectively. Besides, breeding of cr ocodalian species is also done at 
Nandankanan Zoo. The Central

Government has requested the State Gove rnments only to raise such number 
of crocodiles at their breeding centers which can be succesfully rehabilitated 
in the wild. The three sanctuaries iden tified for the purpose in Orissa are 
Satkosia, Bhitarkanik and Hadgarh respectively. Magars have also been 
rehabilited in the river system of Simplipal Tiger Reserve. 
SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, crocodile is one 
of the most important wildlife species. I want to know from the hon. Minister 
as to how many species of crocodiles and magars are seen in the country and 
whether the Government has got any correct statistics of crocodiles and

breeding in Orissa. And, has the number of crocodiles been actually 
increased? I would also like to know whether the Government of India has 
given sanction to any new project. If so, what is the total fund that has been 
given for breeding of crocodiles and also for the protection of crocodile 
sanctuaries? 
MR. CHAIRMAN: How many questions in one supplementary? 
SHRI SURESH PRABHU: Sir, it is not possible to do any physical census 
of the crocodile population in India, and no attempt has ever been made to 
even carry out such a census because, as you know, crocodile is a very 
mobile species which moves from one place to another through various 
riverways, and it is physically impossible and an inconceivable thing to do a 
census of its population. 
SHRI SURESH KESWANI: It has been done in other countries. In fact, as 
you are aware, carrying out even a human population census is a very 
difficult proposition and many countries do not conduct it; but India does it. 
So, this has been the attempt made by the Government since 1970, when this 
Crocodile Conservation Programme was la unched for the first time with the 
help of UNDP, and when the crocod ile population had reached alarmingly 
low levels. 
16 

[20 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
There were only 30 breeding species availa ble at that time. Ever since then, 
various crocodile rearing programmes have resulted in a great success and on 
the basis of which we can say that 5000 Ghariyals, 2300 salt water 
crocodiles and 100 Magars have been released into the wild. The Crocodile 
Conservation Programme, in fact, is ju st a breeding programme where the 
crocodiles are reared in captivity and then released into the wild. This is how 
the programme has, ultimately, proved to be a success. These figures alone 
show that the programme has definitely been a success; we had only thirty 
pairs in 1970 and now so many have been released into the wild. You can 
have any number of crocodiles reared  and there can be any number of 
conservation programmes and sanctuarie s for crocodiles but, ultimately, the 
limiting factor is the capacity of the rivers to absorb them; if the rivers do not 
have the capacity to absorb them, they cannot survive. Unless that is assured, 
there is no point in raising crocodiles in captivity. Otherwise, when they are 
released, they will die. Therefore, th is activity is being carried out under 
different programmes. Now, the Central Government, in the current year, has 
got funds, as you have correctly said, fo r the simple reason that there are not 
many States that are coming forward to  take up this programme. If there is 
any specific proposal from any State Government which would like to take 
up such a programme, the Central Government will definitely consider it on 
the criterion that there should be a possibility of releasing the crocodiles into

Protecting agriculture 
3821. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have approved a proposal to 
provide safeguards to protect domestic agriculture from a surge in imports, 
while seeking to eliminate import subsidies given by developed nations 
under the WTO regime; and 
(b) if so, what are the details of this proposal and its impact on the plight 
of Indian farmers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YE SSO NAIK): (a) and (b) In its initial negotiating 
proposals, submitted to the WTO, in January, 2001, as mandated by Article 
20 of the Agreement, India has demanded separate safeguard measures on the 
lines of the Special Safeguard (SSG) including a provision for imposition of 
Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) in the event of a surge in imports or a decline 
in international prices, as a special and differential (S&D) measure. India has 
also demanded elimination of export subsidies by the developed countries, 
with a view to ensuring its food security and taking care of its livelihood 
concerns. In order to regulate the indiscriminate imports of agricultural 
commodities, the Agreement on Agriculture already provides for suitable 
calibration of the applied rates thereon within the bound rates and initiation 
of trade remedial measures including anti-dumping action, imposition of 
countervailing action or safeguard action under specific circumstances 
provided under the Agreement. The elimination of export subsidies by the 
developed countries and the separate safeguard measures demanded by the 
country in its negotiating proposals will further insulate the domestic farmers 
against the surge of subsidized and indiscriminate imports of agricultural 
products into the country.

Removal of anti-farmer clauses of WTO agreement 
3822. SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH LIBRA: 
SARDAR GURCHARAN SINGH TOHRA: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be  pleased to refer to answer to 
Unstarred Question 1242, given in the Rajya Sabha on the 
3rd August, 2000 and state: 
(a) whether some State Governments have urged the Centre to 
amend or remove some anti-farmer clauses of the WTO agreement; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) and (b) The long-term objective of the 
WTO agreement on Agriculture is to es tablish a fair and market-oriented 
agricultural trading system in the world through a reform process of 
negotiations aiming at correcting and preventing restrictions and distortions 
in the world agricultural markets. 
Article 20 of the WTO agreement on Agriculture mandates negotiations to 
further carry forward the process of re form based on the experiences of the 
implementation of the Agreement. The Government held wide-ranging 
consultations with the different stakeholders including the State 
Governments, to formulate its negotiating proposals. From these 
consultations, the following key issues emerged which need upfront 
addrcssal in the country's negotiating proposals on the WTO agreement on 
Agriculture: 
• To protect its food and livelihood security concerns and to 
secure greater flexibility to support domestic measures for 
agriculture    development,     poverty     alleviation     and    rural 
employment. 
• To create opportunities for expansion of agricultural exports by 
securing meaningful market access in developed countries. 
The country's initial negotiating proposals on Food Security, Market 
Access, Export Competition and Domestic Support, have 
80 

[20 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
been   accordingly   formulated   and   submitted   to   the   WTO   on 
15.1.2001. The Indian proposals aim at. 
• Increasing the flexibility enjoyed by developing countries for 
providing domestic support to the agriculture sector under the 
special and differential provisions as also further strengthening 
of trade defence mechanisms wi th a view to ensuring the food 
security and to take care of livelihood concerns. 
• Demanding of substantial and meaningful reductions in tariffs 
including elimination of peak tariff and tariff escalation, 
substantial reductions in domestic support and elimination of 
export subsidies by the developed countries so as to get 
meaningful market access opportunities.

mouth disease and that farm animals of Punjab, specially of its border villages,

THE    MINISTER    OF    STATE    IN    THE    MINISTRY    OF 
AGRICULTURE (DR. DEBENDRA PRADHAN): (a) and (b) State 
Government of Punjab has informed that the farm animals of Punjab 
specially of its border villages have not got infected with foot and mouth 
disease. However, foot and mouth disease has been reported in Ghaloti 
village of Ludhiana district in the month of February, 2001 wherein out of 
total 2266 cattle and buffaloes, 191 animals were affected of which 29 had 
died. 
(c) Both the State Government of Punjab and Department of Animal 
Husbandry Department Government of India have taken steps to save the 
livestock from foot and mouth disease. 
The State government of Punjab has taken following actions:— 
(i) Vaccination with foot and mouth disease vaccine in the affected area to 
contain the disease. 
(ii) Intensive prophylactic vaccination against FMD in adjoining districts. 
(Hi) Veterinary experts from Punjab Agriculture University, Ludhiana 
and State Animal Health Institute, Jalandhar visited the affected area 
and collected samples for typing of virus. 
(iv) Samples from the affected animals were also sent to Indian Veterinary 
Research Institute. Muktcshwar for confirmation of type of the virus.

RAJYA SABHA [20 April, 2001] 
(v)   Surveillance and monitoring of the disease situation. 
(vi) Notification to Prohibit holding cattle fairs, exhibitions and other 
concentration of animals in the State of Punjab.

following steps:— 
(i) The Department have advised all the State Governments and Union 
Territories to remain vigilant and take necessary steps on war 
footing. 
(ii) The Department has also requested the State Governments which have 
international land border with Pakistan to ensure that livestock and 
livestock products are not brought into the country by land routes at 
borders and to remain vigilant about movement of animals. 
(iii) The States have been advised to undertake vaccination of unaffected 
animals against foot. and mouth disease and to control movement of 
animals. 
(iv) The Department has requested the Ministry of Commerce to ensure 
that importation of livestock and livestock products from United 
Kingdom are not allowed without recommendation of the 
Department. 
(v) The Regional and Animal Quar antine Officers have also been 
instructed to carefully screen all the consignments of livestock and 
livestock products from United Kingdom in order to prevent ingress

† 3829. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
DR. D. MASTHAN:

higher than that in India;

America, Brazil, Australia and India; and 
(c) the reasons for the said differences? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) to (c) Cost of Production depends on cost 
of Cultivation and productivity. Data on Cost of Cultivation is not available in 
respect of Australia and Brazil. As per data furnished by Food and Agricultural 
Organisation (F.A.O.) on Cost of Cultivation and Cost of Production of Wheat in 
U.S.A., it is seen that in the year 1998, the Cost of Cultivation in U.S.A. was 
407 Dollars or Rs. 15124.12 (Based on Exchange rate of Rs. 37.16 per Dollar 
for 1997-98) per hectare. Their average productivity was estimated at 2.8 M. 
Tonnes per hectare and therefore their Cost of Production worked out to 
14.54 Dollars or Rs. 540.15 per quintal. As against this the Cost of Cultivation 
in important Wheat growing States in India like Haryana, M.P., Punjab, Rajasthan 
and U.P. was Rs. 17081.60, Rs. 9365.52, Rs. 17333.89, Rs. 14266.69 and Rs. 
13343.91 per hectare respectively during 1997-98. Accordingly after adjusting 
for productivity and by-product, the Cost of Production in these States worked 
out to Rs. 391.85, Rs. 475.25, Rs. 411.97, Rs. 393.02 and Rs. 362.65 per 
quintal respectively.

THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) Government provides subsidy on urea

objective of making available fertilizers to farmers 
106 

[20 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
at affordable prices and for promoting balanced application of all the three

respective State Governments. Since MRP/indicative MRPs are less than the

payment of subsidy/concession as the difference between the normative cost of 
production plus 12% post tax return on net worth and the MRP/ indicative 
MRPs. While in the case of decontrolle d phosphatic and potassic fertilizers, 
manufacturers are given concession at uniform rates, but in the case of urea, 
which is the only controlled fertilizer, payment of subsidy is determined unit-
wise under the provisions of Retention Price-cum-Subsidy Scheme (RPS).

and other data/details certified by practising CbarteredCost Accountant, 
retention prices of urea units are worked out as per laid down 
principles'parameters approved by th e Fertilizer Industry Co-ordination

private sector, have to maintain their annual accounts that are audited by the 
Chartered Accountants. In the case of public sector companies, such accounts 
are also audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General. Certification by the 
Chartered AccountantCost Accountant of  the company is standard form of 
checking the accounts submitted by the company. Cost data submitted by the 
urea units subject to various checks like notifications giving the details about the 
increase/decrease in prices of inputs, supporting invoices and applying the 
general principles of accounting and arithmetical accuracy. Allocation of cost 
are cross checked for accuracy and intern al consistency from various sources 
like Annual Balance Sheet and Annual Cost Data. 
The fertilizers are sold at uniform MR P and indicative MRPs, as the case 
may be, to the farmers including small and marginal farmers throughout the 
country, which are far less than the cost of production of fertilizers. Thus, the 
benefit is passed on to the

fanners in  the form of uniform and subsidised MRPs/indicative MRPs.

Investigations into Poaching of elephants in Corbett Park 
3866. SHRI KRISHNA  KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether recent investigations into the elephants poaching in Corbett 
National Park recently have shown involv ement of North-East gang's role in 
poaching activities and gross security lapses in checking it; 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof; and 
(c) what action has been taken by Government in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Investigations into the recent 
130 

[20 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
cases of poaching of elephants in Corbett National Park indicate involvement 
of some north-eastern gang in these activities. The arrows recovered from the 
carcass of some elephants are very similar to those used by the Lishu tribe of 
Arunachal Pradesh for hunting of elephants. 
(c) A team of senior wildlife officers of Government of India visited the 
Park on 12-13th February, 2001 to make on the spot assessment of the 
situation. On the basis of the report of the team, the Central Government 
requested the State Government to take the following actions: 
(i) Replace the senior level officers of  the Park with more efficient and 
committed officers. 
(ii)   Fill up all the vacant posts at field level. 
(iii) Improve the communication network to enable the field staff to reach the 
far-flung area of the Park quickly as and when required. 
(iv) The State Government has also been  asked to prepare a contingency plan 
for which the funds can be made available by the Central Government. 
Uttar Pradesh Government has also been requested to transfer the funds 
released by the Central Government for the Park expeditiously to 
Uttranchal Government. 
C.B.I, has also been requested to assist the State Government 
in investigating the case successfully.

Conference of State Forest Ministers 
3869. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PI LLAI: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) what is Government's reaction on the recommendations 7 decisions 
taken in the conference of State Forest  Ministers, held in Coimbatore in 
January, 2000; and 
(b) by when these are likely to be implemented, to protect the Wild Life? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) The National Conference on 
Environment and Forests held on 29-30 January, 2001 at Coimbatore adopted 
the following resolutions for the protection of wild life in the country: 
1. Wild animals do considerable damage to agricultural crops in areas 
adjoining national parks and sanctuarie s, causing considerable concern, 
thereby requiring formulation of an appropriate insurance scheme for 
compensating damage to agricultural crops falling within five kilometers 
of national parks and sanctuaries. 
2. Existing provisions for payment of compensation in the cases of deaths 
due to wild animals were emphasized, with the objective of ensuring 
compaliance by the State/Union Territories Governments. 
3. The ban on recruitment of forestry personnel shall be lifted and the 
vacancies filled up immediately on th e lines of Police Department. The 
field formations shall be reorganized into viable units and be provided 
with adequate mobility, fire arms and effective communication 
network. 
4. An effective mechanism for intelligence gathering and data base of 
habitual offenders should be developed for preventing wildlife crimes. 
134 

[20 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
5. Adequate expertise shall be developed for prosecuting offenders and 
training be organized for undertaking investigations. 
6. Steps shall be taken immediately for designating special courts for 
wildlife offences. 
7. Create    effective    enforcement    infrastructure    both    within 
protected areas and outside protected area to prevent poaching. 
Implementation of these recommendations is the responsibility of State 
Governments. Government of India provides financial and technical 
assistance for infrastructure, weapons,  communication equipments, vehicles 
and conservancy works for mitigating the short comings listed above except 
for placement of staff.

not have any impact on the Glacier?

Helplessness of Railway about safety factors 
3910. SHRI  PREM CHAND  GUPTA: 
SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that, as per a r ecent press report, a Senior Railway 
Board Member (Traffic) has gone on record to say that due to shortage of 
funds, safety factors are getting squ eezed, as maintenance and replacements 
are not carried out in time; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that some statistics quoted that 76 per cent 
accidents are due to derailments and human errors and there are 2000 rail 
fractures and 3000 weld failures per year and the Railways do not have the 
means to check these faults, and are thereby unable to take preventive action; 
and 
173 

RAJYA SABHA [20 April, 2001] 
(c) if so, what are Government's views on these facts? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) Implementation of safety measures and 
replacement of over-aged assets depend upon availability of funds. Railway 
Safety Review Committee in Part -1 of their report had recommended that 
Central Government should give a one time grant of Rs. 15,00(K- crores to 
Railways to wipe out arrears of replacement of over-aged assets. 
While Indian Railways have not recei ved any specific grant from Central 
Government as yet, efforts have been made to suitably enhance the outlay of 
safety related items in the budget. Similarly Railways are progressively 
implementing safety measures within availability of funds and resources. 
(b)   and   (c)  Yes  Sir,   around  34th  of accidents  are  due  to 
derailments and 2/3rd of these are due to human errors of railway staff and 
others. 
Rail fractures and weld failures take place because rails are subjected to 
continuous stresses besides dynamic impact of moving wheels. To overcome 
this problem, instructions from Board's level have been issued to Zonal 
Railways which include augmentation in services of ultrasonic rail flaw detector 
machines for checking rail fractures. Track is being maintained for safe 
running of trains at prescribed speeds. 
Apart from this, following measures have been introduced to ensure 
sturdiness of track and its proper maintenance.

depending upon traffic requirement. 
(ii) Fish plated joints are being re placed with welded joints wherever 
feasible. 
(iii) Steel/wooden sleepers are being replaced with concrete sleepers. 
(iv) More and more track is being brought under mechanised 
maintenance gradually.

drives are also launched to test the alertness of staff.

Rakesh Mohan Committee Report 
3920. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the report of Dr. Rakesh Mohan Committee, which was set up 
in early December, 1998 on financial re structuring of Indian Railways, has 
since been received; 
(b) if not, by when it is likely to be received; 
(c) whether the Committee has recently submitted an Interim Executive 
Summary of its proposed recommendations; 
(d) if so, what are the details thereof; and 
(e) what is Government's decision thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (e) The report of the Expert Group headed 
by Dr. Rakesh Mohan is yet to be r eceived. However, an Interim Executive 
Summary has been received on 17.2.2001. The major recommendations of 
the Interim Executive Summary are: 
1. Institutional separation of rules into policy, regulatory and management 
functions. This will mean: 
(i) Policy makers are limited for setting policy (and paying for 
what they ask for). The Government of India will be in 
charge of setting policy direction. 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [20 April, 2001] 
(ii) Provide operational autonomy and insulate Indian Railways by 
Corporatising it into "Indian Railways Corporation" (IRC). It 
would be governed by a reconstituted Indian Railways Executive 
Board. 
(iii) Set up an Indian Rail Regul atory Authority to regulate IRC's 
activities as a monopoly supplier of rail services particularly 
related to tariff setting. 
2. Ex ante acceptance and commitment by the Government and Indian 
Railways that Indian Railways will operate on commercial lines. Non-
Commercial activities mandated by the Government will be clearly 
demonstrated and Indian Railways appropriately compensated for such 
activities. 
3. In view of financial crisis Indian Railways to pursue the strategic High 
Growth pattern for financial recovery. 
4. Provides exemption from taxation-excise, sales tax etc. for the period of 
transition, say 5 to 7 years. 
5. Set up a Social Safety net to take care of surplus labour. 
6. Restructuring of financial accounts of Indian Railways in accordance 
with the Company's Act, 1956. 
7. Spinning off non-core activities. 
8. Rebalancing of tariffs to eliminate cross subsidisation. 
The Interim Executive Summary is under examination.

Measures to Combat Earthquakes 
† 3935. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn towards the news 
item published in Hindustan dated 18th February, 2001 under the caption 
"Desh Ka Koi bhoobhag bhukamp se surakshit nahi"; 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government in this regard; and 
(c) the details of the effective an d immediate measures taken by 
Government to settle the problems highlighted in the said news-item? 
† Original notice of the question received in Hindi. 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [20 April, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) As per the seismic zoning map prepared by the Bureau of 
Indian Standards (BIS), the country has been divided into five seismic zones. 
Out of these zones, zone 5 is considered  to be the most severe while the zone 
1 is the least. In order to quantify the seismic hazard in  the country, the 
Government has initiated a programme on micro-zonation of the various 
cities located in zones—4 & 5. As a first step in this direction, micro-
zonation of Jabalpur in Madhya Pradesh has been started and is expected to 
be completed in about a year. India Meteorological Department (IMD) has 
recently upgraded its seis mological observational network for better location 
and detection of earthquake activity. Through the scientific studies, building 
codes have been prepared by BIS and are available for use of public. These 
codes need to be adequately used for design & construction of buildings and 
retrofitting of the existing structures.
